taxonomyNote: NM Department of Wildlife calls it Persian ibex (bezoar goat, Persian wild goat); Wikipedia treats the species as wild goat, Capra aegagrus, with the Bezoar ibex (C. a. aegagrus) as a subspecies. NatureServe lists Capra hircus as the domestic form of C. aegagrus and notes Grubb (1993, 2005) included C. aegagrus in C. hircus while Jones et al. (1992) kept them separate.
fieldMarks: About 30 in (76 cm) at the shoulder, hindquarters noticeably higher than the front on flat ground
Mature males up to about 110 lb, females up to about 60 lb; both sexes grow horns (female horns average up to 15 in), male scimitar-shaped horns can exceed 50 in

Light brown in summer; as the rut approaches mature males turn almost white ('white billies') with darkened leg markings, a black-brown cross over shoulders and back, dark face and jet-black beard and tail
behavior: Hooves have a soft inner pocket ringed by a hard rim for clinging to rock; can jump several times their own height
Keen eyesight, notice movement more than half a mile away
Typically do not move much during the night
Seasonal breeding: females bear one to three young in early summer (Pakistan observations)
habitat: Steep, rocky terrain and cliffs (hooves are adapted to it); the New Mexico population lives in the Florida Mountains near Deming. Native habitat is forest, shrubland and rocky areas up to about 3,250 m in Turkey.
range: Native from Turkey and the Caucasus east to Iran, Turkmenistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan. In North America, introduced to the Florida Mountains near Deming, New Mexico in 1970.

lookalikes.name: Feral goat
lookalikes.howToTell: Wild goat is the ancestor of domestic goats; the sources read give no field mark separating the wild form from feral goats.
